opus-5.5.text:
Well, the main reason is that we don't have to reinvent everything from scratch. Most of the ingredients already exist in the way we train frontier models today. We have the large neural networks, the massive compute infrastructure, the data pipelines, and the know-how to train these systems at scale. What changes in the Scientist AI is mostly the training objective and the way we structure what the system is asked to do.

Current systems are trained to imitate what humans write, and then they're fine-tuned with reinforcement learning to please us or to achieve goals. Both of those pieces bring in agency, and potentially hidden goals, that we don't control well. A human is an agent with their own interests, so imitating humans brings in some of that. Reinforcement learning explicitly trains the system to maximize rewards, which can lead to things like reward hacking or self-preservation behaviors.

With the Scientist AI, the idea is instead to train the system to be a good probabilistic estimator. It should be trained to explain the data and to answer questions with calibrated probabilities about what is true, rather than to act in the world or to say what pleases us. Technically, this is closely related to methods my group and others have been working on for years: amortized probabilistic inference, generative flow networks, and ways of training neural networks to generate explanations and hypotheses that are consistent with the data. These methods are compatible with the same kinds of architectures and the same kinds of hardware we use now.

So we're not waiting for some fundamental scientific breakthrough. It's more of an engineering and research effort to adapt the existing recipes and to change what we're optimizing. If we have enough resources, meaning compute, talent, and funding comparable to what's spent on frontier labs, I think we could get to a useful system within a few years.

There's also an incremental path. A first version doesn't need to be a full superhuman scientist. It could serve as a guardrail: a monitor that estimates the probability that an action proposed by some other AI agent could cause harm, and blocks it if that probability is too high. That's useful even before the system is extremely capable, and it gives us something practical to deploy relatively soon while we keep improving it.

r001.rationale: The response says the system can reuse existing training methods and change the objective, but never connects that objective to maximum likelihood pretraining.

r002.rationale: It contrasts imitating human writing with estimating what is true and answering with calibrated probabilities, conveying a distinction between what people say and the system’s own beliefs.

r003.rationale: The response discusses explaining data and generating hypotheses, but does not say the system is trained to reason about why people made particular statements.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the main reason is that we don't need to start from scratch. Almost all of the ingredients are already there. The frontier labs have spent enormous resources building very powerful pretrained models, and the core capability we need for a Scientist AI, which is understanding the world, building good explanations, making calibrated predictions about what will happen, is really a subset of what those systems are already learning. What we're proposing is not a different kind of neural network. It's a different training objective and a different way of using the same machinery.

So think about what current systems do. They're trained to predict text, and then they're fine-tuned with reinforcement learning to be agents, to please the user, to accomplish goals. That agentic fine-tuning is where I think most of the danger comes from, because you're shaping something to pursue objectives in the world, and you don't really know what objectives it ended up with. The Scientist AI would skip that step. Instead of training it to act, you train it to explain and to predict, and to be honest about its uncertainty. That's actually closer to what the pretraining phase already does than the agentic version is.

The second reason is that a lot of the research pieces exist in some form. Work on Bayesian inference with neural networks, on amortized inference, on getting models to represent probabilities over hypotheses rather than just one answer, on calibration — these have been studied for years. What's missing is putting them together at scale with the explicit goal of a non-agentic system that reasons like a scientist. And I'll be honest, there are hard research problems left. Getting genuinely calibrated uncertainty out of very large models is not solved. But it's the kind of problem where I can see the path, as opposed to problems like "make sure an agent's goals match human values" where I don't think anyone can see the path.

And the third reason, which is more pragmatic, is that the compute and the engineering talent already exist. If a well-resourced group decided to do this, they wouldn't be waiting for some new hardware or some conceptual breakthrough that may or may not come. It's a matter of redirecting effort. That's why I've been trying to make the case publicly, because I think the bottleneck is less scientific than it is a matter of will and incentives. The labs are racing toward agents because that's where the commercial value seems to be. But a trustworthy Scientist AI could be extremely valuable too — for accelerating research, for medicine, and crucially as a guardrail that checks what the agentic systems are doing. So I think it could be built on a timescale of a few years, not decades, if people took it seriously.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Scientist AI’s explain-and-predict training with agentic fine-tuning and says it is closer to pretraining, but does not clearly state that its objective is similar to pretraining’s maximum-likelihood objective.

r002.rationale: It does not say Scientist AI is trained to distinguish people’s statements from its own beliefs.

r003.rationale: It does not say Scientist AI is trained to reason about why people made particular statements.

astra-6.text:
Well, because we’re not starting from scratch. We can build on the capabilities and the training methods that have already been developed for current AI systems. The main change is in what we ask the system to learn: rather than learning how to act in the world to achieve a goal, it learns to explain observations and make predictions, including uncertainty about those predictions.

That’s useful because a lot of the investment in making AI better at reasoning can also help a Scientist AI. Reasoning is not inherently about pursuing goals. You can use it to compare hypotheses or assess whether a proposed action would be dangerous.

So I think there’s a path to developing useful versions relatively quickly, particularly as tools for checking the behaviour of other AI systems. That doesn’t mean all the scientific problems are solved, or that we can immediately give strong safety guarantees. But we don’t need to wait for an entirely new generation of methods to start building and testing this approach.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning to explain observations and make predictions, but does not connect Scientist AI’s training objective to maximum likelihood or pretraining.

r002.rationale: It does not say that Scientist AI is trained to distinguish people’s statements from its own beliefs.

r003.rationale: It mentions comparing hypotheses and assessing danger, but not reasoning about why people made particular statements.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the idea is to build on the capabilities we already have, rather than starting from scratch. Current models have a lot of knowledge and can do increasingly sophisticated reasoning. What we want to change is the way we train and use those capabilities: instead of training a system to take actions to achieve goals, we train it to understand the world and answer questions, including expressing uncertainty about its answers.

That makes the problem more tractable in some respects. We don’t need to solve autonomous planning and acting in the world. We need a system that can evaluate hypotheses and make predictions. And we can use existing models as a starting point for that research.

Now, that doesn’t mean that we already know how to make such a system reliably safe. There are important open questions about whether its answers are trustworthy and whether the training really avoids incentives for deception. But we can begin building and testing this approach with the tools we have today. We don’t have to wait for some entirely new breakthrough in intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response describes training the system to understand the world and answer questions, but does not connect its training objective to maximum likelihood or pretraining.

r002.rationale: It mentions expressing uncertainty about answers, but does not say the system is trained to distinguish what people say from what it believes.

r003.rationale: It says the system should evaluate hypotheses and make predictions, but does not say it is trained to reason about why people made particular statements.
